greeting: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. We gather today as a family of faith, held together in the love of the One who calls us by name.
penitential:
Lord, have mercy.
Christ, have mercy.
Lord, have mercy.
psalm_response: I will walk before the Lord, in the land of the living.
homily:
We often think of our lives as a series of accounts—a ledger of what we are owed, what we have given, and what we have lost. We keep track of the slights, the misunderstandings, and the moments when the world didn't treat us with the fairness we expected. We hold these things close, sometimes for years, until they become a weight we carry in the very center of our chest. We believe that if we hold onto these debts, we are somehow maintaining justice, or perhaps protecting ourselves from being hurt again. But the Gospel today asks us to put down the pen. It asks us to stop settling the accounts that only God can truly resolve.

Peter comes to Jesus with a question that feels very human: 'Lord, if my brother sins against me, how often must I forgive? As many as seven times?' Peter is trying to put a limit on grace. He wants a boundary, a number, a point where he can finally say, 'I have done enough. I have been patient enough. The debt is now due.' And Jesus, in that way He has of dismantling our human logic, answers not with a number, but with a horizon: 'Not seven times but seventy-seven times.'

He is not asking us to count. He is asking us to change the way we see. He tells the story of a servant who was forgiven a debt so vast he could never have repaid it in a thousand lifetimes—a debt that would have cost him his freedom, his family, his very life. And yet, the moment he begged for mercy, the master let it all go. The slate was wiped clean. But then, that same servant walks out and finds a fellow servant who owes him a pittance, and he begins to choke him, demanding payment. It is a chilling image. It is the image of a heart that has received infinite mercy but refuses to extend even a drop of it to another.

Why do we do this? Why is it so hard to let go of the things that hurt us? It is because we are afraid. We are afraid that if we forgive, we are admitting that the hurt didn't matter. We are afraid that if we let go of the debt, we are losing our only leverage in a world that feels frequently unfair. But look at what happens to that servant. By holding onto the small debt, he loses his peace. By choosing vengeance over mercy, he ends up in the very prison he tried to build for his brother. He becomes a prisoner of his own resentment.

Benjamin Vo understood something about the freedom of a heart that does not keep score. I think of the way he lived his fifteen years—a boy who was always looking outward, always curious, always ready to share. He didn't live life with a ledger. He lived with a wide-open hand. Think of that moment, so simple and so profound, when he told his parents he wanted to offer his entire piggy bank to help his uncle William. He didn't ask what he would get in return. He didn't ask if it was 'fair.' He didn't worry about the math. He simply saw a need, and his heart, naturally and beautifully, moved toward it. That is the heart of the Kingdom. That is the heart that has been touched by the mercy of God and now reflects it back into the world.

To you, Alan and Thao, I know that for these past three months, the silence in your home has been a heavy, constant companion. You miss the sound of his voice, the way he would greet you in the morning, the way he would giggle when he talked about his 'con chim airlines.' You are living through a season where the math of life feels completely broken. You look at the empty space where his laughter used to be, and you wonder how the world can keep spinning when your own world has been so profoundly changed. It is tempting, in the depth of such grief, to look at the ledger of your own life and wonder why this happened, or to feel a sense of bitterness toward the mystery of it all.

But hear the words of Saint Paul today: 'None of us lives for oneself, and no one dies for oneself. For if we live, we live for the Lord, and if we die, we die for the Lord; so then, whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s.' This is the anchor. You are not holding Ben in your hands anymore; he is being held in the hands of the Lord. And you, too, are held. You are not walking this path alone. You are a family of four, and that bond is not broken by the distance of heaven. It is only changed. It is being held in the eternity of God, where every tear is gathered and every sorrow is known.

I want to speak to those of you who might be carrying a hidden, heavy stone of self-reproach. Maybe you find yourself replaying the past, wondering if you missed something, if you could have done more, if you should have been more watchful. Please, hear this truth today: God does not send these sorrows as a punishment, and He does not hold you responsible for the mysteries of life that are beyond human control. You were the parents Benjamin needed. You were the family he loved. You did not miss anything. You are not being accused by God, and you must not accuse yourselves. Let that stone fall. You are free to grieve, you are free to miss him, but you are not required to carry the weight of 'what if.' That is a burden that Christ has already taken upon Himself. He is the one who says, 'Forgive your neighbor’s injustice; then when you pray, your own sins will be forgiven.' Start by forgiving yourselves. Be as gentle with your own hearts as you were with Benjamin’s.

Ryan, my dear brother, you know that heart better than anyone. You stood shoulder to shoulder with Ben—sharing the sunny days on the water, the cozy moments under the blanket, the dreams of the future. When you feel the quiet, remember that your brother is not a ghost. He is a living, radiant presence in the light of the Lord. He is cheering for you with that same bright, braces-filled smile, watching over you, whispering through the quiet moments to keep dreaming, keep being the kind, curious, brilliant soul that you are. You are a brother, and that is a bond that death cannot touch. You are the one who carries his joy forward into the world.

There is a profound freedom in the mercy that Jesus teaches. It is the freedom to stop being a prisoner of our own past. When we forgive, we are not saying that the hurt was okay; we are saying that we refuse to let the hurt define our future. We are saying that we belong to the Lord, and His mercy is larger than any debt we could ever owe or be owed. Benjamin lived this. He lived with a spirit that was unburdened by the smallness of the world. He was a boy who dreamed of planes that could carry people across oceans, a boy who wanted to build, to connect, to serve. He was a boy who understood that life is a gift to be spent, not a debt to be collected.

Think of the images of him that you hold dear—the sunny day on the yellow boat, the two of you looking out at the airport, the warmth of a winter day shared with family. Those were not just moments; they were glimpses of the Kingdom. They were moments where love was the only thing that mattered. And that love is still real. It is still active. It is still working in the world through the kindness you show to others, through the way you support one another, through the 'Well of Love' that brings clean water to those in need in his name. That is the legacy of a boy who knew that the only way to live is to give.

So, what do you carry out the door today? It is a small thing, but a real thing. When the weight of the loss feels like it is pressing down on your chest, when the urge to hold onto your grief or your questions feels like a shield, take a breath and remember that you are held by the One who forgives seventy-seven times—which is to say, He forgives without limit. You are loved without limit. When you feel the ache, don't try to solve it. Don't try to fix it. Just whisper his name, and then whisper the name of Jesus. Let those two names be your prayer. You are a family of four, and you are being led, step by step, toward a horizon where there are no more debts, no more tears, and no more goodbyes. Only the light. Only the love. Only the reunion that is waiting for you at the end of the journey. Keep walking. Keep loving. Keep trusting. You are not alone. Amen.
spiritual_communion: My Jesus, I believe that You are present in the Most Holy Sacrament. I love You above all things, and I desire to receive You into my soul. Since I cannot at this moment receive You sacramentally, come at least spiritually into my heart. I embrace You as if You were already there and unite myself wholly to You. Never permit me to be separated from You. Amen.
closing: May the Lord bless you and keep you, and may His face shine upon you and give you peace. Amen.
standing_petitions: For our beloved Benjamin, and for all who have gone before us, that they may rest in the eternal light of Christ and find their home in the Banquet of Heaven.
For all who are walking the path of grief, that they may feel the gentle presence of the Lord, find strength in one another, and be comforted by the promise of eternal hope.

readings.label: Reading 1
readings.text:
Wrath and anger are hateful things,
yet the sinner hugs them tight.
The vengeful will suffer the LORD’s vengeance,
for he remembers their sins in detail.
Forgive your neighbor’s injustice;
then when you pray, your own sins will be forgiven.
Could anyone nourish anger against another
and expect healing from the LORD?
Could anyone refuse mercy to another like himself,
can he seek pardon for his own sins?
If one who is but flesh cherishes wrath,
who will forgive his sins?
Remember your last days, set enmity aside;
remember death and decay, and cease from sin!
Think of the commandments, hate not your neighbor;
remember the Most High’s covenant, and overlook faults.

readings.label: Responsorial Psalm
readings.text:
R. (8) The Lord is kind and merciful, slow to anger, and rich in compassion.
Bless the LORD, O my soul;
and all my being, bless his holy name.
Bless the LORD, O my soul,
and forget not all his benefits.
R. The Lord is kind and merciful, slow to anger, and rich in compassion.
He pardons all your iniquities,
heals all your ills.
He redeems your life from destruction,
crowns you with kindness and compassion.
R. The Lord is kind and merciful, slow to anger, and rich in compassion.
He will not always chide,
nor does he keep his wrath forever.
Not according to our sins does he deal with us,
nor does he requite us according to our crimes.
R. The Lord is kind and merciful, slow to anger, and rich in compassion.
For as the heavens are high above the earth,
so surpassing is his kindness toward those who fear him.
As far as the east is from the west,
so far has he put our transgressions from us.
R. The Lord is kind and merciful, slow to anger, and rich in compassion.

readings.label: Reading 2
readings.text:
Brothers and sisters:
None of us lives for oneself, and no one dies for oneself.
For if we live, we live for the Lord,
and if we die, we die for the Lord;
so then, whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s.
For this is why Christ died and came to life,
that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living.

readings.label: Gospel
readings.text:
Peter approached Jesus and asked him,
“Lord, if my brother sins against me,
how often must I forgive?
As many as seven times?” 
Jesus answered, “I say to you, not seven times but seventy-seven times. 
That is why the kingdom of heaven may be likened to a king
who decided to settle accounts with his servants. 
When he began the accounting,
a debtor was brought before him who owed him a huge amount. 
Since he had no way of paying it back,
his master ordered him to be sold,
along with his wife, his children, and all his property,
in payment of the debt. 
At that, the servant fell down, did him homage, and said,
‘Be patient with me, and I will pay you back in full.’
Moved with compassion the master of that servant
let him go and forgave him the loan. 
When that servant had left, he found one of his fellow servants
who owed him a much smaller amount. 
He seized him and started to choke him, demanding,
‘Pay back what you owe.’
Falling to his knees, his fellow servant begged him,
‘Be patient with me, and I will pay you back.’
But he refused. 
Instead, he had the fellow servant put in prison
until he paid back the debt. 
Now when his fellow servants saw what had happened,
they were deeply disturbed, and went to their master
and reported the whole affair. 
His master summoned him and said to him, ‘You wicked servant! 
I forgave you your entire debt because you begged me to. 
Should you not have had pity on your fellow servant,
as I had pity on you?’
Then in anger his master handed him over to the torturers
until he should pay back the whole debt. 
So will my heavenly Father do to you,
unless each of you forgives your brother from your heart.”

pet_prayers.name: Dad
pet_prayers.text:
Hey Ben,

Rafael Rizzo and his little brother Ben really need your help right now. Please bless them with good health and give them the strength to get through this together. Please watch over Brandon and Flor's health, too.

I miss you a whole bunch. I know you're up in heaven watching over all of us. Whenever you're able to, stop by to visit, yeah? I love you and miss you so much!

pet_prayers.text:
Hey Ben - Miss you a whole bunch. Crying all day yesterday, i hope today will be better. Please guide our family through this grief... There's a 14 year old boy that just left earth on August 12... His name is Phero Aden Vo - look for him, maybe you guys can be friends...

Please pray for me and mom to have good health and strength.

I love and miss you Ben

pet_prayers.text: Hey Ben, Trustin visited you today and left you a few airplane cards—we're putting them in your room for you. Please pray for Trustin and his family to stay healthy and strong. Be a guardian angel to Trustin and Ryan as they go through school, and help guide their steps through every year to come.

Ben ơi, Làm cả ngày tới tối, đến lúc chuẩn bị đi ngủ thì nằm một lúc lại nhớ Ben, nhớ mấy chuyện hai anh em từng nói với nhau. Nghĩ tới em, anh thấy buồn nhiều lắm. Ben hãy luôn theo dõi và cầu nguyện cho ba mẹ và Ryan nhé, nước mắt chảy ngược nó khủng khiếp hơn chảy xuôi đó Ben.

Ben ơi, ba nhớ con nhiều quá.

Mommy cũng vậy. Hơn hai tháng rồi mà ba má vẫn khóc mỗi ngày.

Con giúp ba má vượt qua nha, để lo cho em

pet_prayers.text: Hey Ben - need a miracle here. We miss you so much and we’re not sleeping much. Ryan wish you were here, especially this upcoming Saturday to play the new version of Project Flight with him.

pet_prayers.text: Dear Ben, our uncle Thanh has passed away. Please watch over him and pray that his soul finds peace. His saint name is Phêrô. Lord, thank you for sending Chu Thanh into my life. I'll always be grateful for the time he spent tutoring me in math back in high school
